summary: Announces an experimental service that let network users send text to the NIC's Network Journal without logging in to its NLS editing system. Users could submit files from their own computers using mail programs, FTP or Telnet, and the NIC would turn them into journal entries.

plainLanguage.summary: The NIC kept a big shared notebook. This note says you can now mail pages to it from your own computer instead of having to visit and write in it yourself.

questions: how to submit to the nic journal by mail
how to submit to nic journal
subtitle: How to submit articles to the NIC's shared journal and receive delivery notifications over the network.

tldr.problem: Users who wanted to submit to the NIC Journal had to log into the NIC's NLS editing system, which was inconvenient for network users.
tldr.mechanism: The NIC set up a network mail interface that accepts submissions via FTP, Telnet, or local mail systems. Mail with a slash in the username is automatically converted to NLS files, journalized, and sent to specified recipients.
tldr.outcome: Users can now submit journal articles from their own computers and receive citations back via network mail, making the journal accessible to remote users.

facts.label: Processing steps
facts.value: Detect slash, invoke Journal System, convert to NLS, assign number, store, notify

today: RFC 543 describes an early network service. The NIC Journal is no longer active. The concept of remote document submission has evolved into modern collaboration platforms and content management systems.

sections.title: The Network Journal Service
sections.content:
SRI-ARC (Stanford Research Institute's Augmentation Research Center) operates the NIC Journal, a shared repository for network-wide documents. Previously, only users with access to the NIC's NLS (oN-Line System) editing environment could submit articles or receive copies.

RFC 543 announces an experimental system that lets any network user submit documents by mail and receive journal delivery notifications back via the network. Users prepare their text on their own computers using any editor, then submit it to the NIC using standard network mail tools: FTP, Telnet, or their local mail subsystem.
sections.plainLanguage: The NIC kept a shared notebook for the network. Now you can mail articles to it instead of logging in to edit it directly.

sections.title: How to Submit and Receive
sections.content:
To submit an article, a user sends mail to the NIC with a slash (/) in the username field. The part before the slash identifies the author (NIC Ident, or a user's local identity); the part after the slash names the recipients.

Example: jew / mdk dhc means the sender (ident jew) is submitting to recipients mdk and dhc.

The NIC's mail system detects the slash, invokes the Journal System, converts the text to an NLS file, assigns a catalog number, and stores it. All listed recipients are notified. If the slash is absent, the mail is handled normally. Users who prefer can now request automatic delivery of journal citations to their home computer instead of to an NLS file at the NIC.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail with a slash in the username goes to the journal. The sender's name is before the slash, the recipients' names after. The NIC files it, catalogs it, and tells everyone.

sections.title: Available Tools and Methods
sections.content:
The RFC describes three ways to send mail to the NIC: FTP, Telnet, or the local mail subsystem. For TENEX systems using SNDMSG, users append @nic to the username.

Documentation is kept in the NIC's online files under (userguides. journal-netsub,), and paper copies are available. The RFC references RFC 510 for how to configure network delivery of journal mail to a user's home host.
sections.plainLanguage: You can use FTP, Telnet, or your computer's mail program. The NIC recognizes the special username format and does the rest.
